prompt.context: Our client owns a large hotel chain and is thinking about investing in an add-on waterpark on one of its properties. This has been tested in some places and has a lot of potential benefits: family friendly, year-round availability, and potential to bring in new clientele. They have done a lot of work surveying their chain and believe that they have found the right hotel to experiment with a waterpark add-on. Currently, this hotel has a lot of business travelers, but our client believes it would also be attractive for families. Our client is nervous about the capital required to build the add-on and wants to make sure that they are making the right investment.
prompt.question: Should our client invest in the waterpark add-on? How much will the hotel need to charge per room to recoup its costs?

clarifying_info.q: Are there competitors with a waterpark nearby?
clarifying_info.a: There are no competitors immediately nearby for a waterpark, and there is no possibility for a competitive response in the short run.

clarifying_info.q: What do we know about the broader waterpark market?
clarifying_info.a: We do not have any specifics about the market and are unable to conduct additional survey data.
The hotel's normal clientele is business travelers, but the client believes the waterpark will bring in families as well.

clarifying_info.q: What is the investment required and the desired payback period?
clarifying_info.a: The investment is $6 million with a desired payback period of 3 years.

clarifying_info.q: How many rooms does the hotel have?
What is the expected occupancy rate with the waterpark?
clarifying_info.a: With the waterpark, the hotel expects 50% vacancy (i.e., 50% occupancy) on average for the year.
Variable cost is $40 per night per room. The $6 million investment is a fixed cost.

framework: 1. Cost structure: Identify the fixed cost (the $6M investment) and variable costs ($40/night/room), and establish the payback period (3 years).

2. Breakeven analysis: Calculate the minimum room charge needed to recover the fixed investment over 3 years, given expected occupancy; add variable cost to get total required price per room per night.
3. Additional risks and benefits: Qualitative assessment of other revenue streams and potential risks/issues from the investment.

questions.prompt: How much will the hotel need to charge per room per night to recoup its investment within 3 years?
questions.guidance: Candidate should split fixed and variable costs, compute room-nights available per year at 50% occupancy (not 365 days — use 350), then divide annualized fixed cost recovery by annual room-nights to get per-night fixed cost contribution, and add variable cost. Strong candidates will interpret $70/night as a very low breakeven and note the hotel can likely charge a meaningful premium.

math.setup: Fixed cost = $6M investment; payback = 3 years; hotel has 400 rooms; occupancy = 50% (50% vacancy); operating days = 350/year; variable cost = $40/night/room.
steps: Annual room-nights = 400 rooms × 50% occupancy × 350 days = 70,000 room-nights/year
Fixed cost per room per night = $2,000,000 / 70,000 ≈ $28.57, rounded to ~$30/night
Total required charge = $30 (fixed cost component) + $40 (variable cost) = $70/night
math.answer: The hotel needs to charge approximately $70 per room per night to break even on its investment over 3 years.

questions.prompt: How should the client interpret the $70/night breakeven price? What does it imply for the investment decision?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates will recognize that $70/night is extremely low for a hotel with a waterpark amenity, especially one attracting families. The hotel can realistically charge well above this breakeven, implying strong profitability. The client should proceed with the investment.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the potential additional revenue streams and risks/issues associated with the waterpark investment?

categories.name: Additional Revenue Streams
ideas: Charging a separate admission/entry fee for the waterpark
Food and restaurants at the park
Expansion of the waterpark concept to other hotels in the chain

categories.name: Risks and Issues
ideas: Management competency — does the hotel chain have experience running a waterpark?
Regulatory and insurance risks specific to waterparks
Health and litigation risks associated with theme park attractions
Potential competitive response once competitors observe success
Alienating existing business traveler clientele with a family-friendly atmosphere
Seasonal or weather-related demand fluctuations affecting occupancy assumptions

recommendation: The client should proceed with the waterpark investment.
The economics are highly attractive: the breakeven price of ~$70/room/night is low relative to what a hotel with this amenity can realistically charge, leaving substantial margin above breakeven.
The investment opens new family traveler segments and offers additional revenue streams beyond room rates.
risks: Lack of management experience in operating a waterpark could create operational challenges.
Health, safety, and litigation risks are elevated for waterpark facilities and require strong insurance and regulatory compliance.
The family-friendly positioning may alienate the existing business traveler base.
Competitive response, while unlikely in the short run, could erode incremental demand over time.
next_steps: Assess management capability and determine whether to hire specialized waterpark operators or partner with an experienced operator.
Conduct insurance and regulatory due diligence for the specific property.
Develop a pricing strategy (all-inclusive vs. separate admission fee) to maximize revenue above breakeven.
Evaluate replication potential across other hotels in the chain if the pilot succeeds.
